CAV JUDGMENT
(PER: HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE S.G.PANDIT) The above batch of appeals and writ petitions arise
out of common facts and as they involve common questions of law, they are heard together and
disposed of by this common judgment.
2. W.A.No.2476/2015 and connected appeals arise out of learned Single Judge's order dated
10.07.2015 in W.P.No.21216/2014 and connected writ petitions whereby writ petitions are allowed,
striking down the Karnataka Private Aided Educational Institutions Employees (Regulation of Pay,
Pension and Other Benefits) Act, 2014 (for short, 'Act No. 7 of 2014'), holding that the Act No.7 of
2014 is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution of India and encroaches upon the jurisdictional
powers of the Courts, with a further direction to the State to continue to pay salary or pension as the
case may be, as was being paid pursuant to its earlier orders or in other C/W 101 OTHERS words
h1as been paid prior to impugned enactment, with other consequential directions.
3. In W.A.No.100003/2021 and other connected appeals, the challenge is to order dated 24.07.2020
in W.P.No.105439/2014 and W.P.No.108382-417/2014, whereby the learned Single Judge allowed
the writ petitions, quashed the impugned Act No.4 of 2015 i.e., the Karnataka Education
Amendment Act, 2014 (for short, 'Act No. 4 of 2015'), amendment to Section 87 of Karnataka
Education Act, 1983 (for short, 'Act, 1983') with a further direction to the State to consider the cases
of the petitioners to grant additional increment for passing Kannada Language Examination, in
accordance with law.
4. For the sake of convenience, the parties hereinafter are referred to as they stood before the
learned Single Judge. The appellants-State Authorities are referred to as C/W 101 OTHERS
Respondents and respondents herein are referred to as petitioners.
5. Brief facts of the case are that, as stated above, W.A.No.2476/2015 arises out of order dated
10.07.2015 in W.P.No.21216/2014 and connected matters. In W.P.No.21216/2014, the challenge was
to Act No.7 of 2014, whereunder, Section 3 would state that, notwithstanding anything contained in
State Of Karnataka vs Chandrashekar on 24 July, 2026

the Karnataka Education Act, 1983, any order of Government or Rules governing service conditions
of employees of any Educational Institution or any other Law Governing grant-in-aid to the above
employees or any judgment, decree or order of any Court or Tribunal or Authority, the grant-in-aid
admissible to a post held by an employee of private aided educational institution shall be fixed and
calculated at the minimum of pay scale admissible to that post from the date of admission to grant.
Further, it would also state that the service rendered prior to admission for grant-in-aid shall not be
reckoned for the purpose of pay, C/W 101 OTHERS leave, seniority and pension, and further,
finalization of pensionary benefits shall be by non-reckoning the service rendered in non-grant
period as qualifying years. It was the case of the petitioners that they were initially appointed to
teaching or non-teaching posts in private aided institutions by the Management and subsequent to
their appointment, the post in which they were working was admitted to grant-in-aid and thereafter
they requested to count their services prior to admission to grant i.e., from the date of their initial
appointment for the purpose of financial benefits i.e., for the purpose of pay fixation, pension and
pensionary benefits. The petitioners pleaded that this Court on several earlier occasions had held
that the employees of private aided institutions are entitled to count their past services prior to
grant-in-aid for the purpose of pay fixation, pension and pensionary benefits on par with the
government teachers. Those orders were taken up to the Hon'ble Apex Court and the State's Special
Leave Petitions came to be dismissed. Learned Single Judge C/W 101 OTHERS taking note of the
earlier orders, struck down the Act No. 7 of 2014, holding that there was no defect or lacuna in the
enactment to render the judgments already delivered by the Courts to be ineffective, with further

change the law in general, which will affect a class of persons and events at large. It
cannot, however, set aside an individual decision inter partes and affect their rights

the judicial power of the State and to functioning as an appellate court or tribunal."

the Special Arbitration Tribunals in exercise of the State's judicial power conferred upon them which

State would be put to great financial difficulties if the impugned Acts are struck down and any

similar duties cannot be treated unequally. Article 14 of the Constitution of India endeavors that the

treats similarly situated persons unequally is liable to be struck down as violative of Article 14 of the

has to pass the test of intelligible differentia as laid down by the Hon'ble Apex Court in various
decisions and one of them being STATE OF PUNJAB VS. DAVINDER SINGH (2025) 1 SCC 1. The

"85. The Constitution permits valid classification if two conditions are fulfilled. First,
there must be an intelligible differentia which distinguishes C/W 101 OTHERS
persons grouped together from others left out of the group. The phrase "intelligible
differentia" means difference capable of being understood. [See, State of W.B. v.
Anwar Ali Sarkar, (1952) 1 SCC 1 : AIR 1952 SC 75] The difference is capable of being

understood when there is a yardstick to differentiate the class included and others
excluded from the group. [Anwar Ali Sarkar case, (1952) 1 SCC 1 : AIR 1952 SC 75

without a basis and hence, unreasonable. The basis of classification must be
deducible from the provisions of the statute; surrounding circumstances or matters
of common knowledge. [Ram Krishna Dalmia v. S.R. Tendolkar, 1958 SCC OnLine SC
6, para 12 : AIR 1958 SC 538 : 1959 SCR 279] In making the classification, the State is
free to recognise degrees of harm. [Ram Krishna Dalmia case, 1958 SCC OnLine SC 6;
Special Courts Bill, 1978, In re, (1979) 1 SCC 380] Though the classification need not
be mathematical in precision, there must be some difference between the persons
grouped and the persons left out, and the difference must be real and pertinent.
[Moorthy Match Works v. CCE, (1974) 4 SCC 428] The classification is unreasonable
if there is "little or no C/W 101 OTHERS difference". [Deepak Sibal v. Punjab
University, (1989) 2 SCC 145 : 1989 SCC (L&S) 284] Second, the differentia must
have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the law, that is, the

61. It is also necessary to clarify the extent of the relief that would flow from the present judgment.
The issue involved in the present batch of matters is confined to whether the service rendered by
employees during the non-grant period is liable to be reckoned for the purpose of fixation of pay and
other consequential service benefits. Neither the provisions C/W 101 OTHERS governing
grant-in-aid nor the statutory framework casts any liability upon the State to pay salary for the
period prior to admission of the post to grant-in-aid. As produced supra, Annexure-I of Rules, 1999
would make it abundantly clear that the management shall be liable for payment of salary and other
benefits till the date such posts are admitted into grant- in-aid. The liability to pay salary during the
non-grant period continues to rest upon the management of the concerned institution.
Consequently, the service rendered during the said period shall be taken into account only for the
purpose of notional fixation of pay as on the date of admission of the post to grant-in-aid and for
extending consequential benefits such as pension and other service benefits. The employees shall
not be entitled to claim arrears of salary or any other monetary benefits from the State for the period
preceding the admission of the post to grant-in-aid.
